doc.title: Joe Muranyi interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

chapter: Record hunting and the Air Force
title: Enlisting in the Air Force and refusing cryptography school
summary: He enlisted to be a bandsman and turned down an offer to train in cryptography after high test scores.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Wow. And you got to play during your military service, you got to continue to play?

Oh yeah, yeah. So I played in the band and then it was like, I think it was like 1946 or something, and I graduated high school and it was a matter of — when I joined the Air Force the war was still on. The war didn’t technically end until ’47 or something, by treaty or whatever. So I enlisted in ’46 and I’m a veteran of World War II ‘cause the war was still on. But I was going to get drafted. They were still drafting then, they hadn’t changed that law. So I don’t know why — I mean I was always, I’m not a bad businessman but I’m not ahead, I’m not. And somehow I got the information that if you enlisted for three years, and then you would get the GI bill and you could go to college. And if you enlisted then you could pick what you wanted to be. So I enlisted and I wanted to be a bandsman. I was promised that so I enlisted. And I’d go to San Antonio, Texas for, and even then I junk shopped and I found some records. I went over — there’s a river in San Antonio and a couple of waterfalls. I almost went over one of the waterfalls in my khaki outfit with a rowboat or something.

But anyhow, and talking about career choices — will I be an electrician or not — so there I am and I took all the exams and stuff. And one day Private Marino or whatever they called me — “yeah.” “You’ve got to go down to headquarters.” And I thought what did I do? As a matter of fact I did do something when they trained us. You know, hip — hip — hip to the left, right, right oblique, all that kind of stuff. And okay, cigarette break, 15 minutes or something. And we’d all sit down. And I pulled out a book, I’m reading a book, and the sergeant comes over. “What the F are you doing?” I said, “I’m reading a book.” He said, “you’re not allowed to read a book, you’ve got to smoke a cigarette.” I said, “I don’t smoke.” And you know the next day there was a general order on the bulletin board that there will be no reading of books during —. So anyhow, and there were all like rebels, you know, like it was the end of the world. Southerners and you know, from the back woods and all that kind of stuff. So, “Muranyi — Private Muranyi.” I go down, so and so and so, sit down and the officer said, “yes.” There’s a guy, an officer, got a folder with my name. He says, “you know you have a very high IQ.” And I’m flattered, you know, I said, “well yeah, okay.” I’d had tests before and they rated pretty good. And I had gone to Brooklyn Tech which is still to this day considered a very good high school. And I did pretty good. I mean I flunked one of the math courses. It was almost calculus was what it was and non mi piace — I didn’t like it. Anyhow so he says, “you know, we’re always looking for bright young men” he says, “how would you like to go to cryptography school?” So I says, “oh no, no, no, no.” I want to be a clarinet player. I was promised that MOS — military occupation specialty — 508 or whatever it was. And he said, “you know it wouldn’t be bad, we’d send you to Washington and etcetera, etcetera you know. And I said no, no. And I always thought suppose I had said yes.
That’s like figuring out codes and all that.
